demographics.historical_context: Four years after founding. The cemetery serves as one of the only dignified burial grounds for the local Black community during the height of Jim Crow segregation.
The local Black population is growing rapidly. The main commercial avenue is emerging as a center of Black commerce, and the cemetery is becoming the burial ground of the growing middle class.
The aftermath of the 1906 civil unrest and World War I have reshaped the community. The Great Migration is pulling many residents northward, but local institutions are strengthening.
The Great Depression tested the community, but the commercial district thrives. Voter registration drives are gaining momentum and civic organizations are expanding their reach.

The area is becoming a center of the Civil Rights Movement. Many buried here were part of the generations that laid its groundwork — through voter drives, institution building, and community organizing.
The cemetery now spans 100 acres and holds over a century of local Black history. It is a living archive of the community's resilience — from Reconstruction through the Civil Rights era and beyond.
